title: How many classrooms, students and books are there in your school?
description: Tanvi describes her school in Pune with three big counts. The video shows how a part and the number of parts give each count, and says other reasoned answers are fine.
teaching_notes: One idea: estimate a big count from a small part and the number of parts. Many answers are right when the child can explain them.

video_script.why: The child must give three counts about their own school, which differ from child to child.
video_script.substitution: Count one floor, one bench or one shelf, then multiply by the number of such parts.
video_script.anchor: Tanvi describing her school in Pune to her friends
video_script.wrong_answer: I must count every single book
video_script.wrong_move: Chintu thinks every book must be counted one by one. A small part times the number of parts gives a good answer without counting everything.
video_script.payoff_line: a part multiplied by the number of parts

final_answer.value: Sample answer: 24 classrooms, 40 students, 120 books (answers will differ)
final_answer.spoken: for example twenty four classrooms, forty students and one hundred and twenty books, and other reasoned answers are fine

hold_back: Sample answer: 24 classrooms, 40 students, 120 books in a classroom (answers will differ)
never_show: a single right answer for every child
maths_rules: sample school: 8 classrooms on one floor, 3 floors; 8 × 3 = 24 classrooms
sample class: 8 benches, 5 children on each bench; 8 × 5 = 40 students
sample classroom: 4 shelves, about 30 books on each shelf; 4 × 30 = 120 books
other answers are fine when the child can name the part and the number of parts
slip: counting every book one by one is slow and not needed
video_script.design: One idea: a part times the number of parts. Wrong idea: count everything one by one. The three sentences with blanks stay in the anchor band; each blank fills with a sample number on the stage. Open prompt: other reasoned answers are fine.
